claim: PlaF is an integral cytoplasmic membrane-bound enzyme in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Here, we show that catalytically active PlaF is an intrinsic integral membrane protein as it was absent in the soluble fraction of the P. aeruginosa p-plaF (Figure 1a) and remained membrane-associated after treatment of PlaF-containing membranes with denaturation agents (Na2CO3 or urea), which destabilize weak interactions between peripheral proteins and the membrane (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and 1b demonstrating membrane association and resistance to denaturation agents.

claim: PlaF is localized to the cytoplasmic membrane rather than the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa.
source: To identify if PlaF is associated with the inner or outer membrane, P. aeruginosa p-plaF membranes were fractioned by ultracentrifugation in a sucrose density gradient. Western blot analysis of the cytoplasmic membrane protein SecG (Bleves et al., 1996), and the outer membrane-associated Lipid A (Matsushita et al., 1978) combined with PlaF activity measurement revealed that the majority of PlaF was in the cytoplasmic membrane fractions (#9–13) (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by sucrose density gradient fractionation data and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1c, with citations to prior work on SecG and Lipid A.

claim: The catalytic domain of PlaF protrudes into the periplasm.
source: Proteolysis experiments in which P. aeruginosa p-plaF cells with a chemically permeabilized outer membrane were treated with trypsin revealed a time-dependent degradation of PlaF (Figure 1d). These results suggest that PlaF is likely anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane via a transmembrane (TM) domain at the N-terminus predicted from sequence analysis (Kovacic et al., 2016), and its catalytic C-terminal domain protrudes into the periplasm.
evidence: Supported by trypsin proteolysis experiments shown in Figure 1d and sequence analysis cited from Kovacic et al., 2016.

claim: PlaF exhibits phospholipase A1 (PLA1) activity but not PLA2 activity.
source: PlaF, purified with n-octyl-β-D-glucoside (OG) as described previously (Kovacic et al., 2016), showed PLA1 but no PLA2 activity toward the artificial substrates specific to each of these two phospholipase families (Figure 2a) and the natural phospholipid diacyl phosphatidylglycerol containing pentanoic and oleic acid at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with citation to purification method from Kovacic et al., 2016.

claim: PlaF preferentially hydrolyzes glycerophospholipids (GPLs) containing medium-chain fatty acids (C12 and C14).
source: In vitro, purified PlaF preferably hydrolyzed GPLs containing medium-chain FAs (C12 and C14) and showed comparable activities with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), and phosphatidylcholine (PC) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by in vitro enzyme activity data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Deletion of plaF in P. aeruginosa results in significant changes in membrane glycerophospholipid composition.
source: The quantitative mass spectrometric (Q-TOF-MS/MS) analysis of total GPLs isolated from four biological replicates of P. aeruginosa WT, ΔplaF, and ΔplaF::plaF cells revealed significant differences in membrane GPL composition (Figure 2c, Supplementary files 1-3). Statistical analysis of 323 GPL molecular species identified six significantly (p<0.05) accumulating GPLs, varying in the composition of head groups (PE, PG, PC, and phosphatidylinositol, PI), length, and unsaturation of acyl chains, in P. aeruginosa ΔplaF.
evidence: Supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2c and Supplementary files 1-3, with statistical analysis.

claim: PlaF is a major but not the only intracellular PLA1 in P. aeruginosa.
source: The activity assay showed ~90% loss of PLA1 activity in the mutant strain, and restoration of activity in ΔplaF::plaF slightly above the wild-type (WT) level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These findings indicate that PlaF is a major but not the only intracellular PLA1 in P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 demonstrating 90% loss but not complete loss of PLA1 activity in the deletion mutant.

claim: PlaF is involved in the Lands cycle for glycerophospholipid remodeling in bacteria.
source: Our quantitative lipidomics results, which revealed that several PE, PG, and PC molecular species accumulated or were depleted in ΔplaF, together with in vitro PLA activity data of PlaF with various PE, PG, and PC substrates, indicate that PlaF might be a major PLA involved in the Lands cycle (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by lipidomics data and in vitro activity assays, with inference about the Lands cycle role based on the pattern of GPL changes.

claim: P. aeruginosa ΔplaF mutant shows strongly attenuated virulence in Galleria mellonella larvae.
source: The results revealed a remarkable difference in the survival of G. mellonella larvae infected with P. aeruginosa WT or ΔplaF. While ΔplaF was avirulent during 20 hr of infection, the majority of the larvae (~80 %) did not survive 20 hr after infection with the P. aeruginosa WT (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by survival data from G. mellonella infection assays shown in Figure 3a.

claim: P. aeruginosa ΔplaF mutant shows reduced cytotoxicity to bone marrow-derived macrophages compared to wild-type.
source: The viability assays with P. aeruginosa-infected BMDMs showed a significantly (p<0.01) stronger killing effect of P. aeruginosa WT compared to ΔplaF 6 hr after infection (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by BMDM viability assay data shown in Figure 3b with statistical significance.

claim: PlaF is conserved in more than 90% of sequenced P. aeruginosa genomes including clinical isolates.
source: A BLAST search revealed PlaF orthologs in more than 90% of all sequenced P. aeruginosa genomes, including 571 clinical isolates (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by BLAST search results documented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: PlaF homologs are found in other high-priority pathogens including Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: Furthermore, we found PlaF homologs in pathogens from the Pseudomonas genus (P. alcaligenes, P. mendocina, and P. otitidis), and other high-priority pathogens (Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Streptococcus pneumoniae) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The crystal structure of PlaF was determined at 2.0 Å resolution.
source: We present a 2.0-Å-resolution crystal structure of PlaF, the first structure that reveals homodimerization of a single-pass transmembrane (TM) full-length protein.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data collection and refinement statistics provided in Table 1.

claim: PlaF forms a homodimer in the crystal structure.
source: The final model in the asymmetric unit consists of two protein molecules (PlaFA and PlaFB), which are related by improper twofold non-crystallographic symmetry (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Natural fatty acid ligands (myristic acid and undecyclic acid) are bound in the active site of PlaF in the crystal structure.
source: Active site cavities of both the monomers reveal non-covalently bound ligands—myristic acid (MYR), OG, and isopropyl alcohol (IPA) in PlaFA; and undecyclic acid (11A), OG, and IPA in PlaFB (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 5). These FAs are the natural ligands from the homologous organism P. aeruginosa that were co-purified with PlaF, as confirmed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometric (GC-MS) analysis of organic solvent extracts of purified PlaF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4a and GC-MS analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PlaF dimerization is mediated primarily through hydrophobic interactions between transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains.
source: Dimerization is mediated primarily via hydrophobic interactions between symmetry-nonrelated residues from the TM-JM domains of two monomers (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 6), consistent with the hydrophobic effects that dominate in the stabilization of dimeric TM domains (MacKenzie et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4b and Supplementary file 6, with citation to MacKenzie et al., 1997 for context on TM domain dimerization.

claim: The PlaF crystal structure represents the first dimeric structure of a full-length, single-pass transmembrane protein.
source: The full-length PlaF dimer represents a unique structure, as neither a relevant match to the TM-JM helix (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) nor the membrane-spanning coiled-coil structure of the TM-JM dimer has been reported previously.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and knowledge of existing structures.

claim: The catalytic domain of PlaF adopts a canonical α/β-hydrolase fold.
source: The catalytic domain of PlaF adopts a canonical α/β-hydrolase fold (Ollis et al., 1992; Figure 4a) with three α-helices forming a distinct lid-like domain that covers the active site (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4a with citation to Ollis et al., 1992 defining the α/β-hydrolase fold.

claim: The active site of PlaF comprises a catalytic triad with residues S137, D258, and H286.
source: The active site of PlaF comprises the typical serine-hydrolase catalytic triad with S137, D258, and H286 interacting through H-bonds (Jaeger et al., 1994; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis documented in Supplementary file 7 with citation to Jaeger et al., 1994 on serine-hydrolase catalytic triads.

claim: PlaF forms dimers in vivo in P. aeruginosa cells.
source: To investigate the oligomeric state of PlaF in vivo, we performed cross-linking experiments in which intact P. aeruginosa p-plaF cells were incubated with the cell-permeable bi-functional cross-linking reagent dimethyl pimelimidate (DMP). Western blot results revealed the presence of monomeric and dimeric PlaF in DMP-treated cells, whereas dimers were absent in untreated cells (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purified PlaF spontaneously dimerizes in solution.
source: Incubation of this purified PlaF for 90 min with bi-functional cross-linkers of different lengths (DMP; bis(sulfosuccinimidyl) glutarate, BS2G or bis(sulfosuccinimidyl) suberate, BS3) resulted in the formation of a substantial amount of PlaF dimers, suggesting spontaneous dimerization in the solution (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 5b.

claim: PlaF dimerization has a dissociation constant (KD) of 637.9±109.4 nM.
source: The results revealed a sigmoidal binding curve from which a dissociation constant KD=637.9±109.4 nM was calculated, indicating weak binding (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by microscale thermophoresis measurements shown in Figure 5c.

claim: PlaF activity decreases with increasing protein concentration.
source: Measurements of the esterase activity of PlaF samples used for MST experiments revealed that the specific activity of PlaF strongly decreased with increasing PlaF concentrations (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5c.

claim: PlaF activity is regulated through reversible dimerization.
source: The similar dissociation and activation constants support a model in which PlaF activity is regulated through reversible dimerization in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of dissociation constant (KD=637.9±109.4 nM) and activation constant (Kact=916.9±72.4 nM) measured experimentally.

claim: Fatty acids with 10-14 carbon atoms strongly inhibit PlaF activity (>80% inhibition).
source: PlaF was strongly inhibited (>80%) with FAs containing 10–14 carbon atoms (Figure 6a), while the shorter and longer FAs showed only moderate to weak inhibition (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by competitive inhibition assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Decanoic acid (C10 fatty acid) exhibits mixed-type inhibition of PlaF.
source: The results showed that C10 FA lowered maximal hydrolysis rates (vmax) as expected for a competitive inhibitor. Yet, elevated binding constants (Km) in the presence of higher concentrations of C10 FA indicate that PlaF undergoes allosteric changes affecting the binding of FAs (Figure 6b, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by kinetic inhibition studies shown in Figure 6b and Supplementary file 9.

claim: Fatty acids (C10, C11, C12) induce dimerization of PlaF.
source: We examined whether inhibitory FAs affect dimerization by cross-linking of PlaF in the presence of C10, C11, and C12 FAs. The results of SDS-PAGE revealed a significantly higher amount of dimeric PlaF in FA-treated than in untreated samples (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Monomeric PlaF spontaneously tilts toward the membrane in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: However, in 8 and 6 out of 10 simulations started, respectively, from PlaFA or PlaFB, a tilting of the monomer for ~25° toward the membrane was observed (Figure 7b, left and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tilting of monomeric PlaF orients the active site cleft perpendicular to the membrane surface, allowing direct substrate access.
source: This tilting motion cooperatively with rotation of PlaF (Video 1) results in the active site cleft of the catalytic domain being oriented perpendicularly to the membrane surface, such that GPL substrates can have direct access to the active site through the opening at the dimer interface (Figure 7a, right).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7a and Video 1.

claim: The tilted configuration of monomeric PlaF is thermodynamically favored over the non-tilted configuration by 0.66 kcal/mol.
source: The converged and precise (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; SEM<0.4 kcal mol–1) PMF revealed two minima at d=19.6 and 30.6 Å, with t-PlaFA favored over PlaFA by 0.66 kcal mol–1 (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by potential of mean force calculations shown in Figure 7c and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dimeric PlaF is strongly favored over monomeric PlaF with a free energy difference of -11.4 kcal/mol at the dimer interface.
source: The converged (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and precise (SEM<1.4 kcal mol–1) PMF revealed that di-PlaF is strongly favored at r=9.5 Å (–11.4 kcal mol–1) over the monomer (Figure 7d), fitting with the distance of 9.9 Å observed in the crystal structure of PlaF.
evidence: Supported by potential of mean force calculations shown in Figure 7d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under physiological conditions in P. aeruginosa wild-type, between 74% and 96% of PlaF molecules are predicted to be in a monomeric, tilted, catalytically active state.
source: Under such physiological conditions and considering that the equilibria for dimer-to-monomer transition and titling are coupled (Figure 7a), between 74% and 96% of the PlaF molecules are predicted to be in a monomeric, tilted, catalytically active state in P. aeruginosa (Figure 7e).
evidence: Supported by computational predictions based on free energy calculations and estimated PlaF concentrations, shown in Figure 7e.

claim: PlaF is constitutively expressed at low levels in P. aeruginosa wild-type.
source: Our quantitative real-time-PCR results revealed that plaF is constitutively expressed in P. aeruginosa WT at a much lower level than sigma factors rpoD and rpoS (Savli et al., 2003; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 with citation to Savli et al., 2003.

claim: PlaF concentration in P. aeruginosa wild-type is estimated to be 100- to 1000-fold lower than in overexpressing strains.
source: However, the concentration in P. aeruginosa WT is likely 100- to 1000-fold lower, as we could not detect PlaF by Western blot (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from Western blot detection limits shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: PlaF deletion does not significantly affect the growth rate of P. aeruginosa in nutrient-rich medium.
source: Comparison of the growth curves of P. aeruginosa ΔplaF, and the WT in nutrient-rich medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed that PlaF most likely does not reduce virulence by affecting the growth of P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The complemented ΔplaF::plaF strain restores the virulence phenotype lost in the ΔplaF mutant.
source: As expected, the complemented strain (ΔplaF::plaF) restored the loss of virulence of ΔplaF in G. mellonella, and BMDM assays (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: Supported by virulence assay data shown in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: The lid-like domain of PlaF shows higher disorder compared to the catalytic domain.
source: Furthermore, the lid-like domain shows a less ordered structure, as suggested by comparatively higher B-factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by B-factor analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: An intricate ligand-mediated interaction network connects the catalytic site and dimerization site in PlaF.
source: The H-bond interaction of catalytic S137 with the carboxyl group of MYR completes an intricate ligand-mediated interaction network bridging the catalytic (S137) and dimerization (V33) sites in PlaF (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The TM-JM helices of PlaF adopt a coiled-coil-like conformation in the dimer.
source: The TM-JM helices adopt a coiled-coil-like conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), where the αTM1 crosses its counterpart at V14 to form an elongated X-shaped dimer interface with the buried surface area of 656 Å2 per monomer.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spontaneous monomerization of dimeric PlaF was not observed during 2 μs molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Spontaneous monomerization was not observed during the MD simulations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), in line with the sub-nanomolar dissociation constant and the simulation timescale.
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with inference based on the measured dissociation constant.

claim: The free energy barrier for tilting of monomeric PlaF is approximately 1.2 kcal/mol.
source: The free energy barrier of ~1.2 kcal mol–1 explains the rapid transition from PlaFA to t-PlaFA observed in the unbiased MD simulations.
evidence: Inferred from potential of mean force calculations and observed rapid transitions in MD simulations.

claim: The equilibrium constant for PlaF tilting is Ktilting=3.35 with a free energy of ΔGtilting=–0.8±0.2 kcal/mol.
source: The equilibrium constant and free energy of PlaF tilting are Ktilting=3.35 and a ΔGtilting=–0.8±0.2 kcal mol–1.
evidence: Calculated from potential of mean force data.

claim: The free energy of PlaF dimerization is ΔG=–7.5±0.7 kcal/mol under the simulation conditions.
source: From the PMF, the equilibrium constants (Ka=1.57×107 Å2; KX=2.58×105) and free energy (ΔG=–7.5±0.7 kcal mol–1) of PlaF dimerization were computed (Equations 1–3), taking into consideration that KX and ΔG relate to a state of one PlaF dimer in a membrane of 764 lipids, according to our simulation setup.
evidence: Calculated from potential of mean force data using specified equations.

claim: PlaF is likely involved in constant remodeling of membrane glycerophospholipids in wild-type P. aeruginosa.
source: As a catalytically active form of PlaF is favored in the WT, PlaF is likely involved in the constant remodeling of membrane GPLs.
evidence: Inferred from computational predictions showing that the active, tilted monomeric form is favored under physiological conditions.

claim: PlaF might be a promising target for developing novel broad-range antibiotics.
source: These results indicate that PlaF is a novel and potent P. aeruginosa virulence factor, which is conserved in important pathogens and, therefore, might be a promising target for developing novel broad-range antibiotics.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on virulence data and conservation analysis.

claim: The net glycerophospholipid content of wild-type and ΔplaF strains is not significantly different.
source: This may explain why the net GPL contents of the WT and the ΔplaF strain were not significantly (p=0.67) different.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of lipidomics data.

claim: Significantly affected glycerophospholipids in the ΔplaF strain account for approximately 11% (mol/mol) of the total GPL content.
source: Significantly affected GPLs in the ΔplaF strain account for ~11% (mol/mol) of the total GPL content, indicating the profound function of PlaF in membrane GPL remodeling.
evidence: Calculated from lipidomics data.

claim: The six low-abundant glycerophospholipids that accumulate in ΔplaF were not detected in previous lipidomic analyses of P. aeruginosa.
source: Interestingly, these GPLs were present at low concentrations in the cells which may explain why they were not detected in the previous lipidomic analyses of P. aeruginosa GPLs (Benamara et al., 2014; Le Sénéchal et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with prior studies cited (Benamara et al., 2014; Le Sénéchal et al., 2019).

claim: The lid-like domain of PlaF varies significantly among PlaF homologs.
source: Despite the high homology of the catalytic domain, the lid-like domain varies significantly between PlaF homologs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), as observed previously for other lipolytic enzymes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; Chow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 with citation to Chow et al., 2012.

claim: The mechanism of PlaF activation differs from suggested allosteric mechanisms involving structural rearrangements in the juxtamembrane domain.
source: This mechanism, to the best of our knowledge, expands the general understanding of mechanisms of inactivation of integral single-pass TM proteins and differs from suggested allosteric mechanisms implying structural rearrangements (even folding), mostly in the JM domain, upon ligand binding as underlying causes for functional regulation (Bocharov et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with mechanisms described in cited literature (Bocharov et al., 2017).

claim: Overproduction of PlaF in P. aeruginosa is not harmful to the cells.
source: This result can explain the observations that PlaF, an enzyme with membrane-disruptive activity, is found in only very low amounts (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) in WT P. aeruginosa cells and that overproduction of PlaF in P. aeruginosa is not harmful to the cells.
evidence: Inference based on computational predictions and experimental observations of PlaF overexpression.

claim: The area per lipid in a PE:PG=3:1 membrane at 300K is approximately 61 Å2 per leaflet.
source: Considering that the area per lipid in a PE:PG=3:1 membrane at 300K is approximately 61 Å2 per leaflet (or 30.5 Å2 in a bilayer, computed in this work and Murzyn et al., 2005), the total area concentration of PlaF molecules then is
evidence: Calculated from molecular dynamics simulations with citation to Murzyn et al., 2005.

claim: The concentration of PlaF under overexpressing conditions is approximately 5.28×10–4 PlaF monomers per lipid.
source: Experimentally, 40 µg GPLs per 1 ml P. aeruginosa p-plaF (OD580nm 1) were extracted, and a PlaF purification yield of ca. 1 µg from 1 ml P. aeruginosa p-plaF culture with OD580nm was obtained (Bleffert et al., 2019; Supplementary file 3). Considering the molecular weight of PlaF of 35.5 kDa and assuming 750 Da as the average molecular weight of membrane GPL, this relates to a concentration under overexpressing conditions of ~5.28×10–4 PlaF monomers per lipid.
evidence: Calculated from experimental purification yields cited from Bleffert et al., 2019 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Increasing PlaF concentration in the membrane shifts the equilibrium toward dimeric PlaF.
source: Increasing the PlaF concentration in the membrane will thus shift the equilibrium toward di-PlaF.
evidence: Inference based on equilibrium calculations and Le Chatelier's principle.

claim: The crystal structure of PlaF reveals unprecedented details of interactions between membrane-spanning TM-JM domains.
source: The crystal structure of PlaF reveals unprecedented details of interactions between the membrane-spanning TM-JM domains and underlines the role of PlaF for degradation of membrane GPLs.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and comparison with existing knowledge of TM protein structures.

claim: The TM and JM domains of PlaF fold into a long kinked α-helix, which differs from the structure of human EGFR.
source: The TM and JM domains are not distinct but fold into a long kinked α-helix (Figure 4a). This is different from the structure of a human epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), the only structure of an isolated TM-JM domain, in which TM and JM helices are connected by an unstructured loop (Bragin et al., 2016; Endres et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4a with citations to EGFR structures (Bragin et al., 2016; Endres et al., 2013).

claim: Thirteen residues from the catalytic domain of PlaF interact with the JM domain, demonstrating the stabilizing role of the soluble domain on the TM-JM helix.
source: We identified intramolecular interactions of 13 residues from the catalytic domain of PlaF with the JM domain, which clearly demonstrates the stabilizing role of the soluble domain on the TM-JM helix.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis.

claim: The buried surface area of the PlaF dimer interface (656 Å2) is slightly larger than that of the glycophorin TM helix dimer (400 Å2).
source: Sole interactions of TM-JM helices result in the formation of a coiled-coil structure (Figure 4b) that stabilizes the PlaF dimer by burying the surface of 656 Å2, which is slightly larger than the interface of the glycophorin TM helix dimer (400 Å2) without the JM region (MacKenzie et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis with citation to MacKenzie et al., 1997.

claim: Homodimerization mediated via TM-JM interactions was previously shown to be required for activation of single-span TM proteins from receptor tyrosine kinase and ToxR-like transcriptional regulator families.
source: Homodimerization mediated via TM-JM interactions was previously shown to be required for activation of single-span TM proteins from receptor tyrosine kinase (Li and Hristova, 2010) and ToxR-like transcriptional regulator (Buchner et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior studies (Li and Hristova, 2010; Buchner et al., 2015).

claim: The intracellular concentration of fatty acids in E. coli is approximately 2-4 mM.
source: C10–C14 FAs exert competitive inhibition as in vitro effectors of PlaF (Figure 6a) and enhance dimerization (Figure 6c) in the concentration range (0.5–7.5 mM) similar to the intracellular concentration of FAs in E. coli (~2–4 mM) (Lennen et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Lennen et al., 2013.

claim: A configuration similar to tilted PlaF (t-PlaF) was observed for monomeric Saccharomyces cerevisiae lanosterol 14α-demethylase.
source: A configuration similar to t-PlaF was observed for monomeric Saccharomyces cerevisiae lanosterol 14α-demethylase, a single TM spanning protein acting on a membrane-bound substrate (Monk et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Monk et al., 2014.

claim: In tilted PlaF, glycerophospholipid substrates can access the active site cleft directly from the membrane with the sn-1 acyl chain entering first.
source: In t-PlaF, GPL can access the active site cleft directly from the membrane with the sn-1 acyl chain entering the first (Wittgens et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis with citation to Wittgens et al., 2017.

claim: In dimeric PlaF, a glycerophospholipid would need to leave the bilayer into water before entering the active site cleft, which is thermodynamically unfavorable.
source: This is unlikely in di-PlaF, in which the opening of the active site cleft is >5 Å above the membrane (Figure 7e). There, a GPL would need to leave the bilayer into the water before entering the active site cleft, which is thermodynamically unfavorable.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis and thermodynamic principles.

claim: Glycerophospholipid remodeling may play a global role in virulence adaptation in bacteria through simultaneous regulation of virulence-related processes.
source: This class of antibiotics should be potent assuming that GPL remodeling plays a global role in the virulence adaptation in bacteria through simultaneous regulation of virulence-related processes (Benamara et al., 2014; Le Sénéchal et al., 2019; El Khoury et al., 2017; Blanka et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative statement based on cited literature (Benamara et al., 2014; Le Sénéchal et al., 2019; El Khoury et al., 2017; Blanka et al., 2015).

claim: Eukaryotic phospholipases A regulating inflammatory pathways were recently suggested as potential targets of anti-inflammatory drugs.
source: Analogously, eukaryotic PLAs regulating inflammatory pathways through the release of arachidonic acid were recently suggested as potential targets of anti-inflammatory drugs (Mouchlis and Dennis, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Mouchlis and Dennis, 2016.

claim: The Lands cycle involves PLA-catalyzed deacylation of membrane glycerophospholipids to mono-acyl glycerophospholipids followed by lysophospholipid acyltransferase-mediated acylation.
source: This Lands cycle involves PLA-catalyzed deacylation of membrane GPLs to mono-acyl GPLs (lysoGPLs) followed by lysophospholipid acyltransferase (LPLAT)-mediated acylation of lysoGPL to yield a new GPL molecule with acyl chain composition different from the starting GPL (Lands, 1958).
evidence: Cited from Lands, 1958.

claim: It took nearly 50 years after the discovery of the Lands cycle before the enzymes involved in phospholipid remodeling were discovered.
source: Despite the importance of this metabolic process in different animal and plant tissues, it took nearly 50 years before the enzymes involved in phospholipid remodeling were discovered (Shindou and Shimizu, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Shindou and Shimizu, 2009.

claim: Fourteen different mammalian lysophospholipid acyltransferases with specificities for different GPL head groups are involved in the Lands cycle.
source: Fourteen different mammalian LPLAT with specificities for different GPL head groups were reported to be involved in the Lands cycle (Hishikawa et al., 2008; Valentine et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Hishikawa et al., 2008 and Valentine et al., 2022.

claim: The structure of human lysophospholipid acyltransferase provided insights into the molecular mechanism of lysoGPL acylation to GPL.
source: The recently published structure of human LPLAT provided the first insights into the molecular mechanism by which lysoGPL is acylated to GPL (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: At least 16 mammalian phospholipases A that may act on membrane glycerophospholipids with different substrate profiles and tissue expression patterns are known.
source: At least 16 mammalian PLAs (cytosolic and calcium-independent families) that may act on the membrane GPLs with different substrate profiles and tissue expression patterns are known (Clark et al., 1990; Song et al., 1999; Underwood et al., 1998; Ohto et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from Clark et al., 1990; Song et al., 1999; Underwood et al., 1998; Ohto et al., 2005.

claim: Human iPLA2β is allosterically activated by binding to the membrane, which is required to extract a single GPL molecule from the membrane for subsequent hydrolysis.
source: Detailed computational studies revealed that human iPLA2β is allosterically activated by binding to the membrane, which is required to extract a single GPL molecule from the membrane and subsequent hydrolysis (Mouchlis et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Mouchlis et al., 2015.

claim: Periplasmic TesA from Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a multifunctional enzyme with lysoPLA activity but no PLA activity.
source: Previously, we reported that periplasmic TesA from Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a multifunctional enzyme with lysoPLA activity (Kovačić et al., 2013). However, this enzyme has no PLA activity, and therefore it is most likely not related to membrane GPL remodeling (Leščić Ašler et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Kovačić et al., 2013 and Leščić Ašler et al., 2010.

claim: A novel intracellular PLA from P. aeruginosa was recently published whose function for remodeling of GPLs still needs to be experimentally analyzed.
source: We recently published a novel intracellular PLA from P. aeruginosa whose function for remodeling of GPLs still needs to be experimentally analyzed (Weiler et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Weiler et al., 2022.

claim: Comprehensive lipidomic profiling of 113 Escherichia coli strains did not reveal the identity of an intracellular PLA suitable for the Lands cycle.
source: Comprehensive lipidomic profiling of 113 Escherichia coli strains with deleted or overexpressed lipid metabolism genes did not reveal the identity of an intracellular PLA suitable for the Lands cycle (Jeucken et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Jeucken et al., 2019.

claim: Cells steadily adapt their membrane glycerophospholipid composition to changing environmental and developmental conditions.
source: Cells steadily adapt their membrane glycerophospholipid (GPL) composition to changing environmental and developmental conditions.
evidence: General statement supported by knowledge in the field.

claim: The regulation of membrane homeostasis via GPL synthesis in bacteria has been studied in detail.
source: While the regulation of membrane homeostasis via GPL synthesis in bacteria has been studied in detail, the mechanisms underlying the controlled degradation of endogenous GPLs remain unknown.
evidence: General statement based on existing knowledge in the field.

claim: The function of intracellular phospholipases A in GPL remodeling (Lands cycle) in bacteria is not clearly established.
source: Thus far, the function of intracellular phospholipases A (PLAs) in GPL remodeling (Lands cycle) in bacteria is not clearly established.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The adjustment of fatty acid composition of glycerophospholipids upon thermal adaptation represents one of the most important mechanisms of membrane lipid homeostasis.
source: The adjustment of the fatty acid (FA) composition of glycerophospholipids (GPLs) upon thermal adaptation represents one of the most important mechanisms of membrane lipid homeostasis (Sinensky, 1974; Cossins, 1994).
evidence: Cited from Sinensky, 1974 and Cossins, 1994.

claim: De novo synthesis of glycerophospholipids is the main pathway used to tune the proportions of different lipid classes in bacteria.
source: De novo synthesis of GPLs is the main pathway used to tune the proportions of different lipid classes in bacteria (Zhang and Rock, 2008; Jeucken et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Zhang and Rock, 2008 and Jeucken et al., 2019.

claim: Bacteria rapidly alter their membrane GPL composition by chemical modifications (cis-trans isomerization and cyclopropanation) of acyl chains in GPLs.
source: Furthermore, bacteria rapidly alter their membrane GPL composition by chemical modifications (cis-trans isomerization and cyclopropanation) of acyl chains in GPLs to respond to environmental changes (Zhang and Rock, 2008).
evidence: Cited from Zhang and Rock, 2008.

claim: The bacterial pathway for remodeling of GPLs involving rapid turnover of acyl chains is unknown.
source: However, the bacterial pathway for remodeling of GPLs involving a rapid turnover of the acyl chains of GPLs is unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field.
